idiom_name: abstract mapper + one mapper per class (or one discriminating mapper) + a class resolver
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: an abstract mapper declares the mapping protocol (find/load/save/delete) and holds the behaviour common to the whole hierarchy; one concrete mapper per class maps only the columns that class owns and delegates inherited state to the superclass mapper. The table strategy selects the shape - a single table with a discriminator needs one mapper that switches on the type code, class tables need chained per-class mappers (superclass slice first, then the subclass slice of the joined row), concrete tables need independent mappers that tolerate duplicated base columns. A registry or factory resolves the class to instantiate from the discriminator value (or from the object's runtime type), so polymorphic finds hand back the concrete subclass rather than the base type.
code_sketch:
abstract class Mapper:                     # protocol + shared behaviour
    def load(self, row): ...
    def save(self, obj, row): ...

class PaymentMapper(Mapper): ...
class CardPaymentMapper(Mapper):
    def load(self, row):
        obj = super().load(row)                # superclass slice first
        obj.card_number = row['card_number']   # then own columns
        return obj

registry[discriminator(row)] = CardPaymentMapper()   # polymorphic resolve
pitfalls: Skipping the registry and instantiating the base class for every row quietly loses polymorphism - the bug surfaces as missing subclass fields, not as an error.
Letting the mapper shape drift from the table strategy: a per-class mapper hierarchy over a single table duplicates the same row read N times.
No ordering discipline in class-table saving: writing the subclass row before the base row violates the foreign key.
